title: A sequence detector: a gate, and two of the same counter

project.title: Build a sequence detector
project.label: Arming, and what gets turned away

prereqs.why: The last four bits live in a shift register, which is what makes the pattern an input rather than a constant.
Every register here is non-blocking and every output that is not registered is a continuous assignment; mixing the two is how a design ends up a cycle out.
The gate’s outputs are combinational on purpose, and what that costs in path length is why the choice is stated rather than left open.

statement:
**Milestone 3 of 3.** A gate in front of the counter, so the detector
can be armed for one match at a time — and a second counter for what it
turns away.

### The files

```
seq_match.sv    the detector
det_counter.sv  the saturating counter
arm_gate.sv     the gate. New.
seq_detect.sv   the top. Rewired, with three more ports.
```

They are elaborated together, the way a real build does it. A
diagnostic names the file it is in, and clicking it opens that file at
that line.

### arm_gate

```systemverilog
module arm_gate (
    input  logic clk, rst_n,
    input  logic arm,         // a one-cycle pulse
    input  logic found_in,
    output logic found_out,
    output logic missed
);
```

The gate holds one bit of state, call it `armed`.

- `rst_n` is synchronous and active low, and clears `armed`.
- `found_out` is `found_in` while armed; `missed` is `found_in` while
  not armed. Both are **combinational** — this cycle's input against
  this cycle's state, not a cycle later. At most one of them is ever
  high, and only when `found_in` is.
- An `arm` pulse sets `armed`.
- A detection that is passed on **shuts the gate**: `armed` clears.
- **The priority is part of the specification.** Reset beats everything;
  then `arm`; then the self-disarm. So an `arm` pulse arriving on the
  same cycle as a passed detection leaves the gate armed for the next
  one.

### seq_detect, rewired

```systemverilog
module seq_detect #(parameter int W = 4) (
    input  logic clk, rst_n, din, arm,
    input  logic [3:0] pattern,
    output logic found,          // the GATED detection
    output logic missed,
    output logic [W-1:0] count,
    output logic [W-1:0] missed_count,
    output logic sat
);
```

The detector's raw output goes into the gate, not into a counter. The
gate's two outputs drive **two `det_counter` instances** — the same
module, twice, which is why it was made a module.

### Where the arm pulse has to land

`found` is registered, so a match is visible during the cycle *after*
its last bit is clocked in. "An arm pulse on the same cycle as a
detection" therefore means that cycle, not the one the last bit is
presented on. The grading testbench tests exactly that distinction.

### Carrying your work forward

`seq_match.sv` and `det_counter.sv` come with you unchanged if you wrote
them, and arrive worked if you did not.

`seq_detect.sv` is the interesting one. Its port list has **grown**, so
a version carried forward from milestone 2 will not have `arm`,
`missed` or `missed_count` on it, and the testbench will not elaborate
until they are there — the error names the ports that are missing. That
is not a bug in the carry-forward; it is what happens when an interface
changes under a module, and meeting it once here is cheaper than
meeting it for the first time somewhere that matters.
hints: Write the two outputs first, and as continuous assignments rather than inside the clocked block: `found_out = found_in & armed` and `missed = found_in & ~armed`. Registering them delays both by a cycle and every check fails.

The state register is three branches of one if/else-if chain, and the order IS the specification: reset, then arm, then the self-disarm. Swapping the last two changes what happens when an arm pulse and a passed detection coincide.
In the top, give the raw detection a name — `logic raw;` — and wire seq_match's `found` to it. The module's own `found` port is the gate's output, not the detector's.

Two det_counter instances need two different instance names. Give the second one `.sat()` with nothing inside: an output you do not need may be left unconnected, and saying so is clearer than inventing a wire nothing reads.
